title: Theory of Attachment and Place Attachment

findings.consequent: distinction from other affective systems (objects, persons, ideas) and influence on individual equilibrium/well-being
findings.quote: affect related to places therefore exists, and is of a nature that, albeit not fully explicit and defined, nevertheless seems to distinguish it from other affective "systems” (towards objects, persons, ideas, etc.); furthermore it is perceived as one of those important factors that sometimes help and sometimes hinder our equilibrium, our material and spiritual well-being.

findings.antecedent: richness of social interaction (intensity and quality)
findings.consequent: formation of an affective bond (interpersonal)
findings.quote: The formation of an affective bond seems mainly to be a function of the richness of the social interaction (intensity and quality of the interaction) with the person(s) towards whom the attachment behaviour is directed

findings.antecedent: forced transfer from place of residence
findings.consequent: interruption in individuals' sense of continuity, fragmentation of spatial and group identity, sorrow resembling loss of a loved one
findings.quote: the forced transfer from the place of residence represented an interruption in the individuals' sense of continuity, in that it involved the fragmentation of two essential components of identity, namely spatial identity and group identity, which are associated with strong affective elements.

findings.consequent: feeling of belongingness to place and sorrow at moving out of community
findings.quote: length of residence seems to be closely linked both to the feeling of belongingness and to the sorrow at moving out of the community – both of which are also age-linked – while interest in what goes on in the community decreases with age and is linked mainly to socioeconomic class.

findings.antecedent: contemporary society's tendency towards gradual spatial uniformity, increased mobility, and functionalistic relationship with places
findings.consequent: inability to satisfy the fundamental human need for attachment to place
findings.quote: Attachment to place is considered a fundamental human need (Relph, 1976), a need that contemporary society is increasingly unable to satisfy owing to its tendency towards gradual spatial uniformity, increased mobility and hence a purely functionalistic relationship with places.

findings.antecedent: strong affective ties with place of residence
findings.consequent: dysfunctional outcomes, precluding adaptation to new opportunities
findings.quote: strong affective ties with the place of residence may be characteristic of particular groups of population under certain circumstances. Among other things, his work shows how such ties may to some extent prove dysfunctional, precluding adaptation to new opportunities (Fried 2000).

findings.consequent: social involvement, mobility, well-being, mental health, individual hardship, conformist attitudes, social refutation
findings.quote: Also other outcomes of attachment may be postulated at a level of both social involvement and mobility, and at that of well-being and mental health. Moreover, like residential stability, attachment does not necessarily have a positive outcome, but may represent a source of individual hardship, conformist attitudes or social refutation.

findings.consequent: relationship between them (separate concepts vs. components)
findings.quote: the relationship between satisfaction and attachment – that is, whether they are to be considered two separate concepts or whether satisfaction represents a component of or actually coincides with attachment – remains a controversial issue.

findings.consequent: lack of affective bonds with places
findings.quote: although a positive correlation between length of residence and the intensity of attachment to the place of residence is a widely reported finding, the small number of studies in which longitudinal aspects of residential life have been taken into consideration have shown that the causal relationship postulated between high residential mobility and lack of affective bonds with places is far from having been proved.

findings.consequent: affective investment in the neighborhood
findings.quote: relational rootedness (quality and intensity of social bonds), attachment, that is the affective investment made in the neighbourhood of residence, is comparatively unaffected by the length of residence. On the other hand, the modality of arrival in the neighbourhood, or the perception of whether it was a free or a compulsory choice, carries greater weight.

findings.antecedent: high degree of mobility during childhood
findings.consequent: greater desire for stability in adulthood
findings.quote: One further interesting fact is that a high degree of mobility during childhood is associated with a greater desire for stability in adulthood, while global residential mobility does not seem to play any significant role.

findings.antecedent: neighborhood quality, previous experiences, compatibility with residential identity
findings.consequent: affective investment
findings.quote: Affective investment seems to be closely linked to neighbourhood quality, but also to previous experiences and compatibility with residential identity.

findings.antecedent: environments experienced in childhood or adolescence
findings.consequent: strong positive affective bonds
findings.quote: Strong positive affective bonds seem to develop towards the environments experienced in childhood or adolescence, and more occasionally towards environments experienced only in adulthood.

findings.antecedent: unsatisfactory residential experiences during infancy and adolescence
findings.consequent: negative long-term consequences on capacity to form attachments in adulthood
findings.quote: unsatisfactory residential experiences occurring during infancy and adolescence seem to have negative long-term consequences on the capacity to form attachments in adulthood, even towards the more satisfactory environments.

findings.consequent: formation or intensification of affective bonds between occupant and territory
findings.quote: The identifying function is expressed not so much in the form of occupancy and control behaviours but in the personalisation of space, which results in the formation or intensification of affective bonds between occupant and the territory.

findings.consequent: expression of individual identity and stronger feelings of attachment
findings.quote: primary territories are better able to express individual identity and are characterised by stronger feelings of attachment, while secondary territories tend to express a social or group identity.

findings.consequent: attachment to the neighbourhood and development of secondary territoriality
findings.quote: The results of research show that the street layout can facilitate attachment to the neighbourhood and thus the development of a secondary territoriality.

findings.antecedent: attachment associated with expression of identity
findings.consequent: demand for long-term experience with place
findings.quote: not all forms of attachment – in particular that associated with the expression of identity – demand a long term experience with place and that the 'tendency to equate attachment with more permanent residences may have more to do with our cultural bias toward home ownership than with reality' (p. 297).

findings.antecedent: prolonged association between individual and place
findings.consequent: persistency of attachment bond over time
findings.quote: The persistency over time of the bond is a characteristic that also seems to apply perfectly to bonds with places; indeed, prolonged association between an individual and a place is widely recognised as one of the distinctive features of attachment to place.

findings.antecedent: threat to attachment bond with a place
findings.consequent: awareness of attachment
findings.quote: individuals may not be conscious of their attachment to a place (Stokols and Shumaker, 1981; Giuliani, 1991), and only become aware of it under particular circumstances, such as when the bond is threatened.

findings.consequent: particular status in the affective hierarchy
findings.quote: As concerns places, those of childhood often seem to maintain a particular status in the affective hierarchy, but because of the lack of longitudinal studies, there is too little data to be able to formulate precise hypotheses.

findings.consequent: variability in the place of greatest affection (birthplace)
findings.quote: for the vast majority the place of greatest affection is one's birthplace, but there is also a great variability related to mobility experiences and life stages. In addition, only a minority wants to go back and live there.

findings.consequent: strong nostalgic bonds to birthplace without intention to move back
findings.quote: among people who had moved away after the age of 12, there were strong bonds to the birthplace in a "nostalgic” sense, as there was no intention to move back. Among those who had moved away at an earlier age, 'only some warm memories for the former place remained'.

findings.antecedent: desire to remain in contact with attachment figure
findings.consequent: desire for residence stability
findings.quote: The third criterion, that is the desire to remain in contact with the attachment figure, seems to correspond to a desire for residence stability, widely used as one of the indicators of attachment to place.

findings.antecedent: involuntary separation or loss of a loved one
findings.consequent: distress or grief
findings.quote: The criterion complementary to the joy of reunion is the distress provoked by involuntary separation or the grief of loss. The fact that reactions similar to those for the loss of a loved one can be felt in relation to places was the starting point for the considerations on attachment to places and is amply described in all research on displacement (for a review, see Brown and Perkins, 1992).

findings.consequent: homesickness
findings.quote: literature on homesickness (for a review, see Van Tilburg et al., 1996) shows that it occurs frequently among both children and adults (Fisher, 1989; Eurelings-Bontekoe et al. 2000).

findings.consequent: increased presence of symptoms of malaise
findings.quote: a high index of mobility is associated with an increased presence of symptoms of malaise, but also that the relationship between mobility and health is not always negative.

findings.consequent: future mobility
findings.quote: mobility may be a strategy to correct undesirable aspects of one's life and one such undesirable aspect could be lack of attachment, since such a lack is a significant indicator of future mobility.

findings.consequent: seeking of security and comfort
findings.quote: The final, and most important criterion, is the seeking of security and comfort. In environmental literature, the association between place and security has been investigated in particular with reference to the concept of home.

findings.consequent: feelings of security and comfort
findings.quote: Feelings of security and comfort are included among the constituent elements of the experience of home in several empirical research studies (Sixsmith, 1986; Dupuis and Thorns, 1996; Case, 1996; Wiesenfeld, 1997).

findings.consequent: feeling of security (for younger children)
findings.quote: Sebba and Churchman (1986) observed that the feeling of security is perceived as particularly important by the younger children (less than 13 years old) and is not a function of the physical protection offered by the home but of permanence (in Bowlbian terms we could say of accessibility).

findings.consequent: feeling of affection associated with security and family love
findings.quote: The most common form of attachment that emerges is that of a feeling of affection associated with security and family love.

findings.consequent: feeling of comfort
findings.quote: the feeling of comfort appears more and more frequently in women's description of homes.

findings.antecedent: age (childhood, old age vs. adolescence, adult life) and social class (lower classes)
findings.consequent: preponderance of need for security/protection vs. exploration/affiliation/self-expression, and stronger attachment to home/neighborhood
findings.quote: the need for security and protection preponderates during certain stages of life (e.g. childhood and old age), while other needs emerge more forcefully in adolescence and at various stages of adult life (e.g. exploration, affiliation, self-expression, etc.). The strong attachment the elderly display towards the home might thus be seen as the re-emergence of the dominant need for security and protection. Impaired physical resources and the diminished capacity to adapt spatial behaviour patterns to changes in the immediate environment contribute to making the elderly retreat from the novel and seek security. Similarly, the stronger attachment to the neighbourhood found among the lower classes might be accounted for by the continued activation of stress reducing behaviours connected with poverty of resources (Fried 2000).

findings.consequent: similarities in psychological functions (well-being, stage-dependent importance, persistence, sorrow from loss)
findings.quote: Many similarities emerge in the identification of aspects typical of affective relationships between human beings and between persons and places: the importance of the psychological functions performed by these relationships in enhancing the well-being of individuals, the varying importance of particular functions at different stages of one's life, the persistence of the bonds over time, the reactions of sorrow in the case of loss, etc.

findings.consequent: differences
findings.quote: On balance, however, the differences seem to outweigh the similarities.
